title: Distinct differences bound
q:
A set $A$ of positive integers is a Sidon set if all sums $a+b$ with $a\le b$ and $a,b\in A$ are distinct.

Let $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be a Sidon set. Show that the positive differences $a-a'$ with $a,a'\in A$, $a>a'$, are pairwise distinct, and deduce that $|A|<\sqrt{2N}+1$.
source: Elementary counting (proof checked by the reviewer); see K. O'Bryant, A complete annotated bibliography of work related to Sidon sequences, Electron. J. Combin. Dynamic Survey DS11 (2004), arXiv:math/0407117
note: The trivial upper bound; the whole of Erdős #30 is about replacing $\sqrt{2N}$ by $\sqrt N$ plus the smallest possible error.

title: The greedy Sidon sequence grows at most cubically
q:
Let $a_1=1$ and, for $n\ge1$, let $a_{n+1}$ be the least integer greater than $a_n$ such that $\{a_1,\ldots,a_{n+1}\}$ is a Sidon set.

Show that $a_{n+1}\le 4n^3$ for every $n\ge1$, and deduce that there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that the infinite Sidon set $A=\{a_1,a_2,\ldots\}$ satisfies $|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|\ge cN^{1/3}$ for all $N\ge1$.
source: A. M. Mian and S. Chowla, Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. India Sect. A 14 (1944) (the sequence); the cubic bound $a_n\le(n-1)^3+1$ is in A. Stöhr, J. Reine Angew. Math. 194 (1955), see O'Bryant, Electron. J. Combin. Dynamic Survey DS11 (2004) and J. Cilleruelo, Infinite Sidon sequences, arXiv:1209.0326
note: This is the greedy (Mian–Chowla) sequence of Erdős #340; this trivial $N^{1/3}$ bound is still the best known lower bound for it, against the conjectured $N^{1/2-\varepsilon}$.

title: The Erdős–Turán quadratic-residue construction
q:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and, for $0\le k<p$, let $r_k\in\{0,1,\ldots,p-1\}$ be the residue of $k^2$ modulo $p$. Show that
$$A_p=\{\,2pk+r_k : 0\le k<p\,\}$$
is a Sidon set of $p$ elements contained in $\{0,1,\ldots,2p^2-1\}$.

Deduce, using that the ratio of consecutive primes tends to $1$, that the maximum size $h(N)$ of a Sidon set in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfies $h(N)\ge(1/\sqrt2-o(1))\sqrt N$.
source: P. Erdős and P. Turán, On a problem of Sidon in additive number theory, and on some related problems, J. London Math. Soc. 16 (1941), 212–215
note: The first algebraic construction: it shows $h(N)$ really has order $\sqrt N$, leaving only the constant and the error term.

title: Lindström's upper bound
q:
Show that every Sidon set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfies
$$|A|<N^{1/2}+N^{1/4}+1.$$
source: B. Lindström, An inequality for B2-sequences, J. Combinatorial Theory 6 (1969), 211–212; the bound $\sqrt N+O(N^{1/4})$ goes back to Erdős and Turán (1941)
note: Counting differences in short windows replaces $\sqrt{2N}$ by $\sqrt N$; the $N^{1/4}$ error term is the barrier Erdős #30 asks to break.

title: Singer difference sets give asymptotically optimal Sidon sets
q:
Let $q$ be a prime power. Show that there exist $q+1$ residues modulo $m=q^2+q+1$ such that every nonzero residue modulo $m$ is a difference of two of them in exactly one way.

Deduce that $h(q^2+q+1)\ge q+1$, where $h(N)$ is the maximum size of a Sidon subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and, using that consecutive primes $p<p'$ satisfy $p'/p\to1$ together with the upper bound of the previous problem, that $h(N)=(1+o(1))\sqrt N$.
source: J. Singer, A theorem in finite projective geometry and some applications to number theory, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 43 (1938), 377–385
note: Matches the upper bound to first order; at $N=q^2+q+1$ it gives $h(N)\ge\sqrt N+1/2-o(1)$, and Green's Problem 31 asks whether one can beat $\sqrt N+O(1)$ even for infinitely many $N$.

title: B3 sets: counting bound and the Bose–Chowla construction
q:
Call $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ a $B_3$ set if the sums $a+b+c$ with $a\le b\le c$ and $a,b,c\in A$ are all distinct, and let $f(N)$ be the maximum size of a $B_3$ set in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

(a) By counting the sums, show that $f(N)<(18N)^{1/3}$.

(b) Show that for every prime power $q$ there is a $B_3$ set of $q$ integers contained in $\{1,\ldots,q^3-1\}$, and deduce that $f(N)\ge(1-o(1))N^{1/3}$.
source: R. C. Bose and S. Chowla, Theorems in the additive theory of numbers, Comment. Math. Helv. 37 (1962/63), 141–147; the counting bound $(h\cdot h!)^{1/h}N^{1/h}$ is classical, see O'Bryant, Electron. J. Combin. Dynamic Survey DS11 (2004)
note: Gives the right order $N^{1/3}$ for triple sums; Erdős #241 asks whether the lower bound is asymptotically sharp, which needs an upper bound of the form $(1+o(1))N^{1/3}$.

title: Infinite Sidon sets cannot be dense at every scale
q:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ be an infinite Sidon set. Show that there is an absolute constant $C$ (independent of $A$) such that
$$\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{\sqrt{x/\log x}}\le C.$$
In particular $\liminf_{x\to\infty}|A\cap[1,x]|/\sqrt x=0$.
source: Erdős; proof in A. Stöhr, Gelöste und ungelöste Fragen über Basen der natürlichen Zahlenreihe II, J. Reine Angew. Math. 194 (1955), and in Halberstam & Roth, Sequences, Vol. I (1966), Ch. II; see also erdosproblems.com/1191 and O'Bryant, Electron. J. Combin. Dynamic Survey DS11 (2004)
note: An infinite Sidon set must be thinner than finite optimal ones infinitely often; Erdős #1191 asks whether the constant $C$ can be replaced by $0$.

title: Maximal Sidon sets: the cube-root bound and Ruzsa's construction
q:
A Sidon set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is maximal if $A\cup\{x\}$ is not a Sidon set for every $x\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus A$.

(a) Show that there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that every maximal Sidon set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ has $|A|\ge cN^{1/3}$.

(b) Show that there is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every large $N$ there is a maximal Sidon set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $|A|\le C(N\log N)^{1/3}$.
source: Part (a): elementary counting, stated as easy in erdosproblems.com/156; the question comes from P. Erdős, A. Sárközy and V. T. Sós, On sum sets of Sidon sets I, J. Number Theory 47 (1994), 329–347. Part (b): I. Z. Ruzsa, A small maximal Sidon set, Ramanujan J. 2 (1998), 55–58
note: The two bounds differ only by $(\log N)^{1/3}$; Erdős #156 asks whether that logarithm can be removed.

title: Ruzsa's dense infinite Sidon sequence
q:
Show that there is an infinite Sidon set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ such that for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|\ge N^{\sqrt2-1-\varepsilon}$$
for all sufficiently large $N$.
source: I. Z. Ruzsa, An infinite Sidon sequence, J. Number Theory 68 (1998), 63–71
note: Improves the greedy exponent $1/3$ (and Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi's $(N\log N)^{1/3}$, 1981) to $\sqrt2-1\approx0.414$; Erdős #39 asks for every exponent below $1/2$.

title: Balogh–Füredi–Roy: improving the constant in the N^{1/4} term
q:
Show that for all sufficiently large $N$, every Sidon set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfies
$$|A|\le\sqrt N+0.998\,N^{1/4}.$$
source: J. Balogh, Z. Füredi and S. Roy, An upper bound on the size of Sidon sets, Amer. Math. Monthly 130 (2023), no. 5, 437–445; arXiv:2103.15850
note: The first improvement of the constant $1$ in Lindström's $N^{1/4}$ term in over fifty years; Erdős #30 asks to lower the exponent $1/4$ itself to any $\varepsilon>0$.

title: The representation function is never eventually constant
q: Let $A\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ be infinite and let $r(n)=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2: a\le b,\ a+b=n\}$ count representations with $a\le b$. Show that $r(n)$ is not constant for all sufficiently large $n$.
source: G. A. Dirac, Note on a problem in additive number theory, J. London Math. Soc. 26 (1951), 312–313; see M. B. Nathanson, Inverse problems for representation functions in additive number theory, arXiv:0712.0408, Theorem 1
note: The weakest form of the Erdős–Turán philosophy that a representation function cannot be too regular.

title: A basis of order two has at least square-root growth
q:
Let $A\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ be such that every sufficiently large integer can be written as $a+b$ with $a,b\in A$. Show that
$$\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap\{0,1,\ldots,N\}|}{\sqrt N}\ge\sqrt2.$$
source: Elementary counting (proof checked by the reviewer); the order of magnitude $A(x)\gg\sqrt x$ for bases of order $2$ is Theorem 1 of M. B. Nathanson, Cassels bases, arXiv:0905.3144
note: Shows a basis of order $2$ has on average at least a constant number of representations, the starting point of the Erdős–Turán conjecture.

title: A thin basis from binary digits
q: Let $E$ be the set of nonnegative integers whose binary expansion uses only the powers $4^j$ ($j\ge0$), and let $O=2E$ be the set of those using only the powers $2\cdot4^j$. Show that $A=E\cup O$ satisfies $A+A\supseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ and $|A\cap\{0,1,\ldots,N\}|\le4\sqrt N$ for every $N\ge1$.
source: D. Raikov (1937) and A. Stöhr (1937); see M. B. Nathanson, Cassels bases, arXiv:0905.3144, where the bound $A(x)<(2+\sqrt2)\sqrt x$ is shown
note: The square-root lower bound is attained up to a constant, so the Erdős–Turán conjecture cannot follow from counting alone; in this example $r(n)$ is unbounded.

title: Schnirelmann's inequality
q:
For $A\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ let $A(n)=\#\{a\in A:1\le a\le n\}$ and define the Schnirelmann density $\sigma(A)=\inf_{n\ge1}A(n)/n$.

(a) Show that if $0\in A$ and $0\in B$ then $\sigma(A+B)\ge\sigma(A)+\sigma(B)-\sigma(A)\sigma(B)$.

(b) Deduce that if $0\in A$ and $\sigma(A)>0$, then $A$ is a basis of finite order: there is $h$ such that every nonnegative integer is a sum of $h$ elements of $A$.
source: L. G. Schnirelmann (1930); M. B. Nathanson, Additive Number Theory: The Classical Bases, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 164, Springer (1996)
note: The basic density-increment inequality for sumsets, the tool behind Schnirelmann's proof that the primes form a basis of finite order.

title: Erdős's covering-congruence obstruction for 2^k + p
q:
(a) Show that every integer $k$ lies in at least one of the residue classes $0 \bmod 2$, $0 \bmod 3$, $1 \bmod 4$, $3 \bmod 8$, $7 \bmod 12$, $23 \bmod 24$.

(b) Prove that there is an infinite arithmetic progression of odd positive integers none of which can be written as $2^k+p$ with $k\ge0$ an integer and $p$ a prime.
source: P. Erdős, On integers of the form 2^k + p and some related problems, Summa Brasil. Math. 2 (1950), 113–123
note: Contrasts with Romanoff's theorem (1934) that the integers $2^k+p$ have positive lower density; Erdős #16 asks whether such progressions explain all exceptions.

title: Erdős's density increment for adding a basis
q:
Let $\sigma$ denote Schnirelmann density, $\sigma(A)=\inf_{n\ge1}\#\{a\in A:1\le a\le n\}/n$. Let $B\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ with $0\in B$ be a basis of order $k$, i.e. every nonnegative integer is a sum of $k$ elements of $B$. Let $A\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ with $0\in A$ and $\alpha=\sigma(A)$. Show that
$$\sigma(A+B)\ge\alpha+\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{2k}.$$
source: P. Erdős, On the arithmetical density of the sum of two sequences, one of which forms a basis for the integers, Acta Arith. 1 (1936), 197–200
note: This is Erdős #35 with $2k$ in place of $k$; the sharper form follows from Plünnecke's inequality $\sigma(A+B)\ge\alpha^{1-1/k}$ (J. Reine Angew. Math. 243, 1970), since $\alpha^{1-1/k}\ge\alpha+\alpha(1-\alpha)/k$.

title: A basis of order two with logarithmically many representations
q:
Let $r(n)=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2:a+b=n\}$. Show that there exist $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ and constants $0<c_1<c_2$ such that
$$c_1\log n\le r(n)\le c_2\log n$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.
source: P. Erdős, Problems and results in additive number theory, Colloque sur la Théorie des Nombres, Bruxelles 1955, CBRM (1956), 127–137 (the upper bound alone is in P. Erdős, On a problem of Sidon in additive number theory, Acta Sci. Math. (Szeged) 15 (1954), 255–259); extended to every order $h$ by P. Erdős and P. Tetali, Representations of integers as the sum of k terms, Random Structures Algorithms 1 (1990), 245–261
note: Shows the conjectured growth $\log n$ in the strong Erdős–Turán conjecture is attainable; Erdős #66 asks whether $r(n)/\log n$ can even converge to a nonzero limit.

title: Bases of order two have a representation count of at least 8 infinitely often
q: Let $A\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ and $r(n)=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2:a+b=n\}$ (ordered pairs). Suppose $r(n)\ge1$ for every integer $n\ge0$. Show that $r(n)\ge8$ for infinitely many $n$.
source: P. Borwein, S. Choi and F. Chu, An old conjecture of Erdős–Turán on additive bases, Math. Comp. 75 (2006), 475–484; improving the bound 6 of G. Grekos, L. Haddad, C. Helou and J. Pihko, On the Erdős–Turán conjecture, J. Number Theory 102 (2003), 339–352
note: The best known constant lower bound on $\limsup r(n)$; Erdős #28 asks for $\limsup r(n)=\infty$.

title: The Erdős–Fuchs theorem
q:
Let $A\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ be infinite and let $R(N)=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2:a+b\le N\}$. Show that for no constant $c>0$ can one have
$$R(N)=cN+o\!\left(N^{1/4}(\log N)^{-1/2}\right)\quad(N\to\infty).$$
source: P. Erdős and W. H. J. Fuchs, On a problem of additive number theory, J. London Math. Soc. 31 (1956), 67–73
note: Quantifies that the representation function cannot be regular on average, answering a question of Erdős and Turán about $R(N)=cN+O(1)$; the analytic method is a model for attacks on the irregularity problems around Erdős #28 and #66.

title: Gallagher: a prime plus boundedly many powers of 2
source: P. X. Gallagher, Primes and powers of 2, Invent. Math. 29 (1975), 125–142
note: The density version of Erdős #10; the open problem asks for a single $k$ that represents all large integers.

title: Van der Waerden number W(3,2)
q: Show that every colouring of $\{1,2,\ldots,9\}$ with two colours contains a monochromatic $3$-term arithmetic progression, and that this fails for $\{1,2,\ldots,8\}$.
source: R. L. Graham, B. L. Rothschild and J. H. Spencer, Ramsey Theory (2nd ed., 1990)
note: The smallest nontrivial case of van der Waerden's theorem, of which Szemerédi's theorem is the density version.

title: Monotone 3-term progressions in permutations
q:
A monotone $k$-term arithmetic progression in a sequence $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ is a choice of indices $i_1<\cdots<i_k$ such that $x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_k}$ is an arithmetic progression (increasing or decreasing).

(a) Show that for every $n\ge1$ there is a permutation of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with no monotone $3$-term arithmetic progression.

(b) Show that every permutation $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ of the positive integers contains a monotone $3$-term arithmetic progression.
source: J. A. Davis, R. C. Entringer, R. L. Graham and G. J. Simmons, On permutations containing no long arithmetic progressions, Acta Arith. 34 (1977), 81–90
note: The same paper constructs a permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ with no monotone $5$-term progression, leaving $4$ terms as Erdős #196.

title: A progression-free set from ternary digits
q: Let $r_3(N)$ be the maximum size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ containing no three distinct elements in arithmetic progression. Show that the set of $n\ge1$ such that $n-1$ has only digits $0$ and $1$ in base $3$ contains no $3$-term arithmetic progression, and deduce that $r_3(N)\ge\tfrac12N^{\log2/\log3}$ for all $N\ge1$.
source: P. Erdős and P. Turán, On some sequences of integers, J. London Math. Soc. 11 (1936), 261–264
note: The first construction in the paper that introduced $r_k(N)$; it shows progression-free sets can have polynomial size.

title: Behrend's construction
q:
Show that there is a constant $c>0$ such that for all $N\ge2$ there is a set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $3$-term arithmetic progression and
$$|A|\ge N\exp\!\left(-c\sqrt{\log N}\right).$$
source: F. A. Behrend, On sets of integers which contain no three terms in arithmetical progression, Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. USA 32 (1946), 331–332
note: Shows $r_3(N)=N^{1-o(1)}$, so any upper bound must leave room for this; it is still essentially the best lower bound.

title: Roth's theorem
q: Show that there is a constant $C$ such that for all $N\ge3$ every subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $3$-term arithmetic progression has at most $CN/\log\log N$ elements.
source: K. F. Roth, On certain sets of integers, J. London Math. Soc. 28 (1953), 104–109
note: The $k=3$ case of Erdős #139 by Fourier-analytic density increment, the method all later 3-AP bounds refine.

title: Szemerédi's theorem
q: Let $k\ge3$ and let $r_k(N)$ be the maximum size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $k$-term arithmetic progression. Show that $r_k(N)=o(N)$ as $N\to\infty$; equivalently, every subset of $\mathbb{N}$ of positive upper density contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.
source: E. Szemerédi, On sets of integers containing no k elements in arithmetic progression, Acta Arith. 27 (1975), 199–245
note: This is Erdős #139, now solved; Erdős #3 asks for arbitrarily long progressions under the much weaker hypothesis $\sum_{n\in A}1/n=\infty$, and all later work on it is about the rate in $r_k(N)=o(N)$.

title: Gowers's quantitative Szemerédi theorem
q: Let $k\ge3$ and $c_k=2^{-2^{k+9}}$. Show that for all sufficiently large $N$, every subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $k$-term arithmetic progression has at most $N(\log\log N)^{-c_k}$ elements.
source: W. T. Gowers, A new proof of Szemerédi's theorem, Geom. Funct. Anal. 11 (2001), 465–588
note: The first bound for all $k$ with a reasonable rate, introducing the Gowers uniformity norms.

title: Kelley–Meka bounds for 3-term progressions
q:
Show that there is a constant $c>0$ such that for all $N\ge3$ every subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $3$-term arithmetic progression has at most
$$N\exp\!\left(-c(\log N)^{1/12}\right)$$
elements. Deduce that every $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ with $\sum_{n\in A}1/n=\infty$ contains a $3$-term arithmetic progression.
source: Z. Kelley and R. Meka, Strong bounds for 3-progressions, FOCS 2023, arXiv:2302.05537 (the exponent $1/12$ is made explicit in T. F. Bloom and O. Sisask, The Kelley–Meka bounds for sets free of three-term arithmetic progressions, Essent. Number Theory 2 (2023), arXiv:2302.07211); exponent improved to $1/9$ by T. F. Bloom and O. Sisask, An improvement to the Kelley–Meka bounds on three-term arithmetic progressions, arXiv:2309.02353
note: Answers Green's Problem 9, gives a new proof of the $k=3$ case of Erdős #3 (first proved by Bloom and Sisask in 2020), and brings the upper bound to the same shape as Behrend's lower bound, with exponent $1/12$ against $1/2$.

title: Leng–Sah–Sawhney bounds for long progressions
q:
Let $k\ge5$. Show that there is a constant $c_k>0$ such that for all sufficiently large $N$, every subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $k$-term arithmetic progression has at most
$$N\exp\!\left(-(\log\log N)^{c_k}\right)$$
elements.
source: J. Leng, A. Sah and M. Sawhney, Improved bounds for Szemerédi's theorem, arXiv:2402.17995 (2024)
note: The first bound for $k\ge5$ beating every power of $\log\log N$; Erdős #3 for $k$-term progressions would follow from a bound $r_k(N)\ll N/(\log N)^{1+\delta}$ for some $\delta>0$.

title: The Green–Tao theorem
q: Show that for every $k\ge3$ the primes contain a $k$-term arithmetic progression.
source: B. Green and T. Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Ann. of Math. 167 (2008), 481–547
note: A relative Szemerédi theorem for the primes, which have density zero; Erdős #141 asks for such progressions among consecutive primes, and #200 for the length of the longest one below $N$.

title: Sumsets of integers: the trivial bound and its equality case
q:
Let $A$ be a finite nonempty set of integers and $A+A=\{a+b : a,b\in A\}$. Prove that $$|A+A|\ge 2|A|-1.$$

Show moreover that equality holds if and only if $A$ is an arithmetic progression.
source: M. B. Nathanson, Additive Number Theory: Inverse Problems and the Geometry of Sumsets, GTM 165, Springer (1996), Ch. 1
note: The simplest direct theorem together with its inverse theorem: extremal sumset size forces arithmetic structure.

title: The Cauchy–Davenport theorem
q: Let $p$ be a prime and let $A,B$ be nonempty subsets of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. Prove that $$|A+B|\ge \min\big(p,\ |A|+|B|-1\big).$$
source: A.-L. Cauchy (1813); H. Davenport, On the addition of residue classes, J. London Math. Soc. 10 (1935)
note: Transfers the integer bound to a cyclic group of prime order, where wrap-around is the only obstruction.

title: Ruzsa's triangle inequality
q:
Let $A,B,C$ be finite nonempty subsets of an abelian group. Prove that $$|A|\,|B-C|\le |A-B|\,|A-C|.$$

Deduce that $d(X,Y)=\log\dfrac{|X-Y|}{\sqrt{|X|\,|Y|}}$ satisfies $d(B,C)\le d(A,B)+d(A,C)$.
source: I. Z. Ruzsa (1978); T. Tao and V. Vu, Additive Combinatorics, Cambridge University Press (2006)
note: First tool for passing information about one sumset to another; an injection argument rather than a counting identity.

title: Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality
q: Let $A,B$ be finite nonempty subsets of an abelian group with $|A+B|\le K|A|$. Prove that for all integers $m,n\ge 0$ with $m+n\ge 1$, $$|mB-nB|\le K^{m+n}|A|,$$ where $mB-nB$ is the set of all $b_1+\cdots+b_m-b'_1-\cdots-b'_n$ with $b_i,b'_j\in B$.
source: G. Petridis, New proofs of Plünnecke-type estimates for product sets in groups, Combinatorica 32 (2012), 721–733 (inequality due to Plünnecke 1970 and Ruzsa 1989)
note: Small doubling propagates to all iterated sum and difference sets with polynomial loss; used in every Freiman-type theorem below.

title: Bogolyubov's lemma in the finite field model
q: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$ have density $\alpha=|A|/2^n>0$. Prove that $A+A+A+A$ contains a subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ of codimension at most $\alpha^{-2}$.
source: N. N. Bogolyubov (1939); B. Green, Finite field models in additive combinatorics, Surveys in Combinatorics 2005, LMS Lecture Note Series 327, §10
note: The basic Fourier-analytic argument (large spectrum plus Parseval); Green's Problem 50 asks to improve the codimension from $\alpha^{-2}$ to $O(\log(1/\alpha))$.

title: The Erdős–Heilbronn conjecture for restricted sums
q: Let $p$ be a prime and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ be nonempty. Writing $A\hat{+}A=\{a+b : a,b\in A,\ a\neq b\}$, prove that $$|A\hat{+}A|\ge \min\big(p,\ 2|A|-3\big).$$
source: J. A. Dias da Silva and Y. O. Hamidoune, Cyclic spaces for Grassmann derivatives and additive theory, Bull. London Math. Soc. 26 (1994); polynomial-method proof: N. Alon, M. B. Nathanson and I. Z. Ruzsa, Adding distinct congruence classes modulo a prime, Amer. Math. Monthly 102 (1995)
note: Restricting to distinct summands breaks the Cauchy–Davenport proofs; the polynomial method handles it and settles Erdős Problem 476.

title: Freiman's 3k−4 theorem
q: Let $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$ be finite with $|A|=k\ge 3$ and $$|A+A|\le 3k-4.$$ Prove that $A$ is contained in an arithmetic progression of length at most $|A+A|-k+1$.
source: G. A. Freiman (1959); see M. B. Nathanson, Additive Number Theory: Inverse Problems and the Geometry of Sumsets, GTM 165 (1996), Ch. 1
note: The first genuinely structural inverse theorem: doubling below 3 forces containment in a short progression.

title: Ruzsa's Freiman theorem in groups of exponent 2
q: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$ be nonempty with $|A+A|\le K|A|$. Prove that $A$ is contained in a subspace $H\le\mathbb{F}_2^n$ with $$|H|\le K^2\,2^{K^4}\,|A|.$$
source: I. Z. Ruzsa, An analog of Freiman's theorem in groups, Astérisque 258 (1999), 323–326 (proved there for groups of torsion $r$, with bound $K^2r^{K^4}|A|$)
note: Freiman's theorem in the model setting with an exponential loss in $K$; Marton's conjecture (Green's Problem 49) asks for polynomial loss.

title: Sanders' quasi-polynomial Bogolyubov lemma
q: Prove that there is an absolute constant $C$ such that the following holds. If $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$ has density $\alpha>0$, then $A+A+A+A$ contains a subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ of codimension at most $C\log^4(2/\alpha)$.
source: T. Sanders, On the Bogolyubov–Ruzsa lemma, Analysis & PDE 5 (2012), 627–655, arXiv:1011.0107 (Theorem A.1)
note: Replaces $\alpha^{-2}$ by a power of $\log(1/\alpha)$ via almost-periodicity; the conjectured codimension in Green's Problem 50 is $O(\log(1/\alpha))$.

title: Marton's conjecture (polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa) over F_2
q: Prove that there is an absolute constant $C$ (one may take $C=12$) such that the following holds. If $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$ is nonempty with $|A+A|\le K|A|$, then $A$ is covered by at most $2K^{C}$ cosets of some subgroup $H\le\mathbb{F}_2^n$ with $|H|\le|A|$.
source: W. T. Gowers, B. Green, F. Manners and T. Tao, On a conjecture of Marton, Ann. of Math. 201 (2025), 515–549, arXiv:2311.05762 (2023)
note: Polynomial dependence on $K$, solving Green's Problem 49; its Bogolyubov-type analogue (Problem 50) remains open.

title: Schur's theorem with an explicit bound
q: Let $k\ge1$ and $N\ge\lfloor e\cdot k!\rfloor$. Prove that for every colouring of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $k$ colours there exist $x,y,z$ of the same colour (not necessarily distinct) with $x+y=z$.
source: I. Schur (1916); R. L. Graham, B. L. Rothschild and J. H. Spencer, Ramsey Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley (1990)
note: Reduces to multicolour Ramsey numbers of triangles via the colouring of pairs by differences; gives the factorial upper bound in Erdős Problem 483.

title: The Schur number S(3) = 13
q: Show that $\{1,\ldots,13\}$ can be coloured with $3$ colours so that no colour class contains $x,y,z$ (not necessarily distinct) with $x+y=z$, but that every $3$-colouring of $\{1,\ldots,14\}$ contains such a monochromatic solution.
source: B. M. Landman and A. Robertson, Ramsey Theory on the Integers, AMS Student Mathematical Library (2004)
note: An exact small case, showing how far the general factorial bound is from the truth.

title: Exponential lower bound for Schur numbers
q: Let $S(k)$ be the largest $N$ such that $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ admits a $k$-colouring with no monochromatic solution of $x+y=z$ ($x,y$ not necessarily distinct). Prove that $S(k+1)\ge 3S(k)+1$ for every $k\ge1$, and deduce that $$S(k)\ge\frac{3^k-1}{2}.$$
source: I. Schur (1916); R. L. Graham, B. L. Rothschild and J. H. Spencer, Ramsey Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley (1990)
note: The matching lower-bound construction; Erdős Problem 483 asks whether the true growth is exponential, i.e. whether $S(k)<c^k$.

title: Colourings that defeat a non-regular linear equation
q:
Let $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ be nonzero integers such that $\sum_{i\in I}a_i\neq0$ for every nonempty $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and let $p$ be a prime with $p>\sum_{i=1}^k|a_i|$. Colour each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ by the last nonzero digit of $n$ in base $p$.

Prove that this colouring with $p-1$ colours has no monochromatic solution of $a_1x_1+\cdots+a_kx_k=0$.
source: R. Rado, Studien zur Kombinatorik, Math. Z. 36 (1933); R. L. Graham, B. L. Rothschild and J. H. Spencer, Ramsey Theory, 2nd ed. (1990)
note: The necessity half of Rado's theorem; the number of colours depends on the size of the coefficients, and Green's Problem 21 asks whether it can be bounded in terms of $k$ alone.

title: Van der Waerden's theorem
q: Prove that for all integers $k,r\ge1$ there exists $N$ such that every colouring of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $r$ colours contains a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length $k$.
source: B. L. van der Waerden, Beweis einer Baudetschen Vermutung, Nieuw Arch. Wisk. 15 (1927)
note: The colour-focusing induction, the engine behind Rado's sufficiency proof and finite-sums theorems.

title: Folkman's finite sums theorem
q: Prove that for all integers $r,m\ge1$ there exists $N$ such that for every $r$-colouring of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ there is a set $S$ of $m$ distinct positive integers such that all sums $\sum_{s\in T}s$, over nonempty $T\subseteq S$, lie in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ and have the same colour.
source: J. Folkman, R. Rado, J. Sanders; R. L. Graham, B. L. Rothschild and J. H. Spencer, Ramsey Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley (1990)
note: Finite version of Hindman's theorem; Erdős Problem 532 is the infinite version for two colours.

title: Rado's theorem for a single equation
q: Let $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ be nonzero integers. Prove that every finite colouring of $\mathbb{N}$ admits a monochromatic solution $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ of $$a_1x_1+\cdots+a_kx_k=0$$ if and only if $\sum_{i\in I}a_i=0$ for some nonempty $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$.
source: R. Rado, Studien zur Kombinatorik, Math. Z. 36 (1933)
note: Completes the characterisation of partition regular single equations; the boundedness question in Green's Problem 21 concerns the complementary case.

title: Rado's boundedness conjecture for three variables
q: Let $a_1,a_2,a_3$ be nonzero integers such that $\sum_{i\in I}a_i\neq0$ for every nonempty $I\subseteq\{1,2,3\}$. Prove that $\mathbb{N}$ can be coloured with $24$ colours so that there is no monochromatic solution of $$a_1x_1+a_2x_2+a_3x_3=0.$$
source: J. Fox and D. J. Kleitman, On Rado's boundedness conjecture, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 113 (2006), 84–100
note: The case $k=3$ of Green's Problem 21 with a bound independent of the coefficients; open for $k\ge4$.

title: Monochromatic x, x+y and xy
q: Prove that for every finite colouring of $\mathbb{N}$ there exist $x,y\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x$, $x+y$ and $xy$ all have the same colour.
source: J. Moreira, Monochromatic sums and products in N, Ann. of Math. 185 (2017), 1069–1090
note: Forces a sum and a product into one colour (together with $x$); Green's Problem 22 asks the same for the pair $x+y$, $xy$ alone (with $x,y\ge3$ to exclude $2+2=2\cdot2$), which remains open.

title: Partition regularity of Pythagorean pairs
q: Prove that for every finite colouring of $\mathbb{N}$ there exist distinct $x,y\in\mathbb{N}$ of the same colour such that $x^2+y^2$ is a perfect square.
source: N. Frantzikinakis, O. Klurman and J. Moreira, Partition regularity of Pythagorean pairs, Forum Math. Pi 13 (2025), e5, arXiv:2309.10636
note: Settles Green's Problem 23 via multiplicative functions; partition regularity of $x^2+y^2=z^2$ with $x,y,z$ all of one colour remains open for general finite colourings.

title: Discrepancy 1 survives exactly to length 11
q:
For $f:\{1,\ldots,N\}\to\{-1,1\}$ let $D(f)=\max\{|\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(kd)| : n,d\ge1,\ nd\le N\}$.

Show that some $f:\{1,\ldots,11\}\to\{-1,1\}$ has $D(f)=1$, but that every $f:\{1,\ldots,12\}\to\{-1,1\}$ has $D(f)\ge2$.
source: Folklore; the value 11 is a(1) in OEIS A237695 (maximum length of a ±1 sequence of discrepancy n), whose a(2)=1160 is due to B. Konev and A. Lisitsa, A SAT attack on the Erdős discrepancy conjecture, arXiv:1402.2184 (2014)
note: The case $C=1$ of the Erdős discrepancy problem by hand; the case $C=2$ already needed a SAT solver.

title: Weyl equidistribution and the quantifier in Khinchin's question
q:
Let $\alpha$ be irrational. Prove that for every interval $[a,b)\subseteq[0,1)$, $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\#\{1\le k\le n : \{k\alpha\}\in[a,b)\}=b-a.$$

Show on the other hand that for every real $\alpha$ there is a measurable $E\subseteq(0,1)$ with $\lambda(E)=1$ such that $\{k\alpha\}\notin E$ for all $k\ge1$.
source: H. Weyl, Über die Gleichverteilung von Zahlen mod. Eins, Math. Ann. 77 (1916); L. Kuipers and H. Niederreiter, Uniform Distribution of Sequences, Wiley (1974)
note: Equidistribution holds for intervals, but no single $\alpha$ works for all measurable sets, so Khinchin's question in Erdős Problem 994 must be read as: for each fixed $E$, for almost all $\alpha$.

title: Exponential sums of a sequence cannot all stay bounded
q: Let $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ be any sequence of real numbers and $e(t)=e^{2\pi it}$. Prove that $$\limsup_{k\to\infty}\ \sup_{n\ge1}\ \Big|\sum_{j=1}^{n}e(kx_j)\Big|=\infty.$$
source: Remark of P. Erdős (1964), recorded at erdosproblems.com/987 (where it is described as easy), together with the later results of Clunie (1967)
note: The version with $\sup_n$ is elementary; Erdős Problem 987 asks the same with $\limsup_n$ in place of $\sup_n$, and for the growth rate in $k$.

title: A multiplicative sequence with logarithmic discrepancy
q: Let $\lambda:\mathbb{N}\to\{-1,1\}$ be the completely multiplicative function with $\lambda(3)=1$, $\lambda(p)=1$ for primes $p\equiv1\pmod 3$ and $\lambda(p)=-1$ for primes $p\equiv2\pmod 3$. Prove that $$0\le\sum_{k=1}^{n}\lambda(k)\le\log_3 n+1\quad\text{for all } n\ge1,$$ and deduce that $|\sum_{k=1}^{n}\lambda(kd)|\le\log_3 N+1$ whenever $n,d\ge1$ and $nd\le N$.
source: P. Borwein, S. K. K. Choi and M. Coons, Completely multiplicative functions taking values in {−1,1}, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 362 (2010), 6279–6291 (Corollary 4)
note: Shows that discrepancy along homogeneous progressions can grow as slowly as $\log N$, matching the lower bound $\gg\log N$ that Erdős conjectured.

title: Random colourings of pairs: the upper bound n^{3/2}
q: For $f:\{(x,y): 1\le x<y\le n\}\to\{-1,1\}$ and $X\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ write $f(X)=\sum_{x<y,\ x,y\in X}f(x,y)$. Prove that there is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every $n\ge1$ some $f$ satisfies $|f(X)|\le Cn^{3/2}$ for all $X\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$.
source: P. Erdős (1963), as recorded at erdosproblems.com/1028; the method is the standard Chernoff-plus-union-bound argument, see N. Alon and J. H. Spencer, The Probabilistic Method
note: Random colouring plus a union bound over all $2^n$ sets gives the upper bound in Erdős Problem 1028.

title: Roth's theorem on discrepancy in arithmetic progressions
q: Prove that there is a constant $c>0$ such that for every $N\ge1$ and every $f:\{1,\ldots,N\}\to\{-1,1\}$ there is an arithmetic progression $P\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $$\Big|\sum_{x\in P}f(x)\Big|\ge cN^{1/4}.$$
source: K. F. Roth, Remark concerning integer sequences, Acta Arith. 9 (1964); the exponent 1/4 is sharp by J. Matoušek and J. Spencer, Discrepancy in arithmetic progressions, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 9 (1996)
note: For all progressions (not only homogeneous ones) discrepancy is polynomial, in contrast with the logarithmic example above.

title: Erdős–Spencer lower bound for imbalance of 2-colourings of pairs
q: With $f(X)$ as above, prove that there is a constant $c>0$ such that for every $n\ge2$ and every $f:\{(x,y): 1\le x<y\le n\}\to\{-1,1\}$ there is $X\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $|f(X)|\ge cn^{3/2}$.
source: P. Erdős and J. Spencer, Imbalances in k-colorations, Networks 1 (1971/72), 379–385
note: Matches the random upper bound, giving $H(n)\asymp n^{3/2}$ in Erdős Problem 1028; the density version for large induced subgraphs is Erdős Problem 162.

title: Spencer's six standard deviations
q: Prove that there is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every $n\ge1$ and any $n$ sets $S_1,\ldots,S_n\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ there exists $\chi:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{-1,1\}$ with $$\Big|\sum_{x\in S_i}\chi(x)\Big|\le C\sqrt n\quad\text{for all } 1\le i\le n.$$
source: J. Spencer, Six standard deviations suffice, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 289 (1985) (with $C=6$)
note: Beats random colouring (which gives $\sqrt{2n\log(2n)}$) by partial colouring and entropy; the prototype of all sharp discrepancy bounds.

title: Law of the iterated logarithm for lacunary exponential sums
q:
Let $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ be positive integers with $n_{k+1}/n_k\ge q$ for all $k$, for some fixed $q>1$. Prove that for almost every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, $$\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{|\sum_{k=1}^{N}e(n_k\alpha)|}{\sqrt{N\log\log N}}\le1.$$

Deduce that if $f$ is a trigonometric polynomial with $\int_0^1f=0$, then for almost every $\alpha$, $$\sum_{k=1}^{N}f(\{\alpha n_k\})=O\big(\sqrt{N\log\log N}\big),$$ and in particular this sum is $o(N\sqrt{\log\log N})$.
source: P. Erdős and I. S. Gál, On the law of the iterated logarithm I, II, Nederl. Akad. Wetensch. Proc. Ser. A 58 = Indag. Math. 17 (1955), 65–76, 77–84 (they prove the limsup equals 1)
note: Answers Erdős Problem 995 for trigonometric polynomials; the open case is general $f\in L^2$, where Erdős constructed examples whose sums exceed $N(\log\log N)^{1/2-\epsilon}$ infinitely often.

title: The Erdős discrepancy problem, Hilbert-space form
q:
Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and $f:\mathbb{N}\to H$ a function with $\|f(n)\|=1$ for all $n$. Prove that $$\sup_{n,d\ge1}\Big\|\sum_{j=1}^{n}f(jd)\Big\|=\infty.$$

In particular, every $f:\mathbb{N}\to\{-1,1\}$ has unbounded discrepancy along homogeneous arithmetic progressions.
source: T. Tao, The Erdős discrepancy problem, Discrete Analysis 2016:1, arXiv:1509.05363
note: Reduction to completely multiplicative functions plus a logarithmically averaged Elliott conjecture; the conjectured $\log N$ growth rate remains open.
